claims.assertion: The driver drove 24.9 km against an optimal route of 21.8 km, i.e. 3.1 km (+14%) further than the shortest and most direct route.
There are two off-route segments on the GPS track: 22:57–23:03 added 1.14 km (drifting up to 970 m off the optimal route) and 23:21–23:24 added 1.51 km (up to 985 m off).
No traffic incident on the optimal route was recorded during the trip window, so no segment is excused by a road-closure/accident justification.

The only congestion record is speed band 3 (20–29 km/h) on East Coast Parkway and Airport Boulevard; band 3 is not band 1 or 2, and in any case a speed band cannot waive a segment on its own, so it cannot excuse either off-route segment.

The chat log contains no request from the rider and no driver message announcing or agreeing a route change before the driver left the optimal route; the rider's only message concerns the pickup point, so the segments are not passenger-agreed deviations.

The driver's written statement that he simply followed a GPS reroute is not a policy excuse: the GPS instruction post-dates the deviation and no pre-departure agreement exists, and it is contradicted by the GPS record of two distinct off-route segments.

This is a RydeTAXI trip billed on the meter, so the unexcused extra distance passed straight into the fare: the fare record shows 3.1 excess km billed at $1.41/km = $4.41, inside a total of $53.58 (distance $35.17 for 24.9 km, time $13.04 for 50.2 min).

Because the unexcused segments (1.14 km + 1.51 km = 2.65 km) account for the whole billed excess of 3.1 km within the 0.25 km mapping residual, the rider should be refunded the metered cost of that excess distance: 2.65 km × $1.41/km = $3.74.

The driver's account already carries one upheld dispute in the last 90 days and this case makes a route deviation established against him, which is the situation in which an account-review flag is added.

weaknesses: The excess is only 3.1 km (+14%) with two short segments, so the driver will argue it is ordinary GPS-driven routing rather than a deliberate detour (F1, F3, F4).

East Coast Parkway and Airport Boulevard were running at speed band 3 (20–29 km/h) for the whole trip window, and the 50.2 min actual duration vs 28 min estimate lets the driver argue he was avoiding slow roads even though no incident was recorded (F11, F12, F2, F13).
The rider's own chat messages contain no objection to the route and no request to keep to the shortest road, so the driver may characterise the rider's silence as acquiescence (F8, F9).

The time component ($13.04 for 50.2 min) and the unexcused-segment share of it are not recoverable under the metered-distance refund rule, so the rider recovers well under the full $4.41 excess (F7, F5, RD-2).
The rider's profile shows 2 disputes in 90 days with 0 upheld, which the other side may use to suggest a pattern of claims (F15, F5).

events.title: Proposed ruling: refund_partial $3.74 (model confidence 0.93)
events.body:
This is a route_deviation dispute on a completed RydeTAXI metered trip, so the metered-distance branch of RD-2 governs: the fare tracks distance, and unexplained extra distance passed straight into the meter [F1][F7][RD-2]. The GPS record shows two off-route segments: 22:57-23:03 driven 2.63 km against an optimal 1.50 km, +1.14 km [F3], and 23:21-23:24 driven 1.65 km against an optimal 0.14 km, +1.51 km [F4]; each is an off-route segment requiring an exemption under RD-1 [RD-1].

events.body:
RIDER: We reviewed your fare for this trip and found the route taken wasn't the best one for part of the journey. The GPS record shows two stretches where the distance driven was well over the shortest reasonable route, and the driver's congestion explanation didn't cover it. You'll receive a $3.74 Ryde voucher for the extra distance on those stretches. It will be added to your Ryde account. The time charge and platform fee aren't distance-based, so they stay. Nothing changes on your account.

DRIVER: We reviewed a route dispute on this trip and found part of the distance driven was off the best route. The GPS record shows two stretches with noticeably more distance than the shortest reasonable route, and the congestion on the highway and airport road doesn't exempt those stretches. A $3.74 Ryde voucher is being issued to the rider for that extra distance. This is recorded as a route breach on your file. No account flag or suspension applies from this case.

claims.assertion: The driver drove 24.9 km against an optimal route of 21.8 km, i.e. 3.1 km (+14%) further than the shortest and most direct route.
There are two off-route segments on the GPS track: 22:57–23:03 added 1.14 km (drifting up to 970 m off the optimal route) and 23:21–23:24 added 1.51 km (up to 985 m off).
No traffic incident on the optimal route was recorded during the trip window, so no segment is excused by a road-closure/accident justification.

The only congestion record is speed band 3 (20–29 km/h) on East Coast Parkway and Airport Boulevard; band 3 is not band 1 or 2, and in any case a speed band cannot waive a segment on its own, so it cannot excuse either off-route segment.

The chat log contains no request from the rider and no driver message announcing or agreeing a route change before the driver left the optimal route; the rider's only message concerns the pickup point, so the segments are not passenger-agreed deviations.

The driver's written statement that he simply followed a GPS reroute is not a policy excuse: the GPS instruction post-dates the deviation and no pre-departure agreement exists, and it is contradicted by the GPS record of two distinct off-route segments.

This is a RydeTAXI trip billed on the meter, so the unexcused extra distance passed straight into the fare: the fare record shows 3.1 excess km billed at $1.41/km = $4.41, inside a total of $53.58 (distance $35.17 for 24.9 km, time $13.04 for 50.2 min).

Because the unexcused segments (1.14 km + 1.51 km = 2.65 km) account for the whole billed excess of 3.1 km within the 0.25 km mapping residual, the rider should be refunded the metered cost of that excess distance: 2.65 km × $1.41/km = $3.74.

The driver's account already carries one upheld dispute in the last 90 days and this case makes a route deviation established against him, which is the situation in which an account-review flag is added.

weaknesses: The excess is only 3.1 km (+14%) with two short segments, so the driver will argue it is ordinary GPS-driven routing rather than a deliberate detour (F1, F3, F4).

East Coast Parkway and Airport Boulevard were running at speed band 3 (20–29 km/h) for the whole trip window, and the 50.2 min actual duration vs 28 min estimate lets the driver argue he was avoiding slow roads even though no incident was recorded (F11, F12, F2, F13).
The rider's own chat messages contain no objection to the route and no request to keep to the shortest road, so the driver may characterise the rider's silence as acquiescence (F8, F9).

The time component ($13.04 for 50.2 min) and the unexcused-segment share of it are not recoverable under the metered-distance refund rule, so the rider recovers well under the full $4.41 excess (F7, F5, RD-2).
The rider's profile shows 2 disputes in 90 days with 0 upheld, which the other side may use to suggest a pattern of claims (F15, F5).

claims.assertion: Both off-route segments in this trip are short and arose in slow traffic on the two main corridors, and the recorded traffic picture during the whole trip window was only band 3 (20–29 km/h) on East Coast Parkway and Airport Boulevard; the driver's position is that a GPS reroute in these conditions is a reasonable cause for the deviation. This is a mitigation argument only: the policy does not permit that position to succeed.

No traffic incident (accident, roadwork, breakdown, block, heavy traffic) is recorded anywhere near the optimal route during the trip window, so no off-route segment qualifies for the RD-4(a) exemption.

The chat log contains no message in which the driver proposed a different route before leaving the optimal route and no message in which the rider agreed to one; the driver's only pre-trip message concerns arrival and vehicle details, so no segment is exempt under RD-5.

The two off-route segments added 1.14 km (22:57–23:03) and 1.51 km (23:21–23:24) respectively, a total of 2.65 km of excess metered distance; as a RydeTAXI trip the fare is metered, so this excess distance passes directly into the fare.

At the trip's rate of $1.41 per km, the refund exposure on the two unexempted segments is 2.65 km × $1.41 = $3.74, and it is limited to distance units only: the 50.2 min time charge of $13.04 and the $1.47 platform fee are not refundable under RD-2.

The rider's framing that the whole 3.1 km gap should be refunded is not the correct measure: the fare fact shows the billed excess of 3.1 km ($4.41), while RD-2 refunds only the sum of the unexempted off-route segment extra_km (2.65 km), the residual difference being map-matching residue.
The driver has no prior upheld route-deviation dispute in the last 90 days (route: 0), so this dispute does not make him a 'repeated' route offender and no flag_account is warranted.
The driver's account is 5.7 years old with 1165 trips in 90 days and 4.53 rating, which supports treating this as an isolated routing lapse rather than a pattern of fare abuse.

weaknesses: The GPS record itself establishes both off-route segments (F3: +1.14 km, F4: +1.51 km) and no exemption applies: F13 shows no traffic incident on the optimal route, and F11/F12 are only band 3 (20–29 km/h), which under RD-4(b) is corroborative at most and cannot exempt a segment on its own — so the rider's refund on the unexempted distance is likely to be upheld.

The chat facts contain no agreement: F8 and F9 are only pickup logistics and F10 is the driver's own statement 'I followed my GPS; it rerouted me' — no pre-deviation proposal by the driver and no rider consent, so RD-5 cannot rescue any segment.

The driver's statement (F10) that 'nothing wrong with the fare' cannot be built on, because it conflicts with the system GPS and fare records (F1, F3, F4, F5), which win; and F2 (50.2 min vs 28 min estimated) will be used by the rider to argue a deliberate detour, even though time charge is not refundable under RD-2.
F16 records 1 upheld dispute in 90 days, so the rider may argue RD-6's 90-day pattern language applies even though the upheld case is not a route deviation (route: 0).

points.response: Conceded as a mitigation-only point: band 3 (20-29 km/h) is not band 1 or 2, and a speed band alone cannot exempt a segment, so the driver's "reasonable cause" argument cannot remove either off-route segment from my refund.
Agreed and it is my case too: with no incident near the optimal route in the trip window, neither the 1.14 km segment nor the 1.51 km segment is exempt.
Agreed: the only messages are pickup logistics and the driver's post-hoc GPS explanation, so no segment is exempt under the pre-deviation agreement rule.
Accepted, and it confirms liability: the 2.65 km of unexempted off-route distance on a metered RydeTAXI trip passes directly into the fare.

Accepted without reservation - $3.74 is exactly my requested figure, computed as 2.65 km x $1.41/km from the fare record's per-km rate, and I do not claim the $13.04 time charge or the $1.47 platform fee.
Accepted: my claim is the clause-correct one, 2.65 km of unexempted segments, not the whole 3.1 km billed excess, the 0.45 km difference being within the mapping residue.
This does not defeat my flag request: the profile shows the driver already has 1 upheld dispute in the last 90 days, and the flag is an additional account-review action, not the finding itself.

The driver's long record explains the small size of the refund but does not cure the deviation; the profile shows 2 disputes with 1 upheld in 90 days, so it cannot be presented as an unblemished pattern.

Conceded on the distance figure: the GPS record does show 24.9 km against 21.8 km optimal (F1), but RD-1 does not treat the 3.1 km headline gap as the compensable sum — only the two unexempted off-route segments count (F3, F4), so C1 overstates the refundable base.
Conceded: the two segments and their extra_km are on the GPS record (F3: 1.14 km; F4: 1.51 km) and my client does not dispute them; they total 2.65 km, not the 3.1 km the rider claims.
Conceded: no traffic incident near the optimal route is recorded in the trip window (F13), so no segment is excused under RD-4(a).

Accepted as to legal effect, and it is common ground that band 3 (20–29 km/h) is not band 1 or 2 and alone cannot exempt a segment (F11, F12); this is exactly why my client does not seek exemption but asks the tribunal to limit the refund to distance units only, consistent with RD-4(c) and RD-2.

Conceded: the chat shows only pickup logistics, so no segment is waived by passenger agreement under RD-3(a) or RD-5 (F8, F9); I note the same absence means the rider did not request a different route either, which is neutral rather than incriminating.

Conceded that F10 is no excuse: a post-deviation GPS instruction cannot constitute a pre-departure agreement under RD-5, and the statement must yield to the GPS record of the two segments (F10, F3, F4).

Accepted that this is a metered RydeTAXI trip and that excess distance enters the fare (F7), but the fare record shows the billed excess is 3.1 km = $4.41 (F5) while RD-2 refunds only the sum of unexempted segment extra_km, so the rider's own figure of $4.41 is not the recoverable amount.

Agreed on the arithmetic: 2.65 km × $1.41/km = $3.74, and this matches my own requested outcome, so there is no dispute on quantum — RD-2 limits the refund to the distance units of the unexempted segments (F3, F4, F5, F7).

Contested: RD-6 requires the prior upheld dispute to be a route matter, and F16 records route: 0 with the single upheld dispute of another type; with no prior uphold for route deviation, this case does not make my client 'repeated' and no flag_account should be added.
